summary: TARS is a VS Code extension (LangGraph planner, syntax check, self-critique loop) that explains a selected Java snippet or open file. It conditions the prompt on a questionnaire-based developer profile (expertise, role, style) and can retrieve from project documentation. In a within-subjects lab study (18 participants, 4 comment-stripped CodeSearchNet Java snippets, GPT-4.1 Nano, no-AI control), correctness did not differ (cosine 0.888 vs 0.886) and the 26% time reduction was not significant (p=0.085). Workload and personalisation were rated only in the TARS condition, against a scale midpoint.

claims.claim: Participants using TARS completed tasks 26% faster
claims.evidence: Table I: 224 s vs 304 s; Mann-Whitney U=494.5, p=0.085, not significant. The test treats the 36 observations per condition as independent samples even though the design is within-subjects; no paired analysis or effect size. The abstract states the speed-up as a finding.

claims.claim: TARS lowers cognitive load (intro: 'significantly lower cognitive workload than the manual condition')
claims.evidence: Table II is labelled 'TARS condition only': NASA-TLX was never collected for the manual condition, so no between-condition comparison exists. Table II means (Mental Demand 3.64, Frustration 3.86, Effort 3.01 on 1-5) sit at or above the midpoint, yet §V-B reports them as significantly below it (t=-3.69, -2.94, -5.91). These are internally inconsistent unless unstated reverse coding was applied.

claims.claim: Explanations are meaningfully adapted to each developer's profile
claims.evidence: §V-C: mean of 9 custom author-written items is 3.92 vs midpoint 3; there is no non-personalised arm, so the effect of the Theory-of-Mind profile is untested; some participants reported verbosity not matching their stated preference. This is evidence of perception only.

claims.claim: Correctness is comparable across conditions ('accelerator, not corrector')
claims.evidence: Cosine 0.888 vs 0.886, t(16)=-1.52, p=0.18. The degrees of freedom are inconsistent with 18 paired participants, and the e5-embedding cosine is compressed into a 0.88-0.89 band that cannot discriminate. Unblinded author grading: Fully Correct 7 vs 4, Not Correct 2 vs 3. An underpowered null.

patterns.note: Explanation-as-comprehension-aid vs a no-AI control: no measurable comprehension gain (cosine 0.888 vs 0.886; Fully Correct 7 vs 4 by unblinded author grading), time -26% but p=0.085. No retention or no-tool follow-up task, so nothing about deskilling either way. The control cannot isolate personalisation or in-IDE anchoring from 'any LLM explanation'.
In-IDE agent that explains a highlighted snippet or the whole open file; snippet-level only, with no repository navigation or cross-file questions evaluated.
RAG over local project documentation is described, but the study snippets are from CodeSearchNet with no project docs, so retrieval was never exercised.
Critique node self-reviews explanations up to a retry cap; not evaluated.

methodology.sample: 18 participants (practitioners, researchers, students; per-group counts not reported); 4 Java snippets (CodeSearchNet, cyclomatic complexity 10-30, comments removed); 2 snippets per condition, 36 observations per condition
methodology.baselines: No AI assistance; no generic LLM chat arm and no non-personalised TARS arm
methodology.variance: SDs for time and cosine; unpaired t-test and Mann-Whitney despite a within-subjects design; no CIs or effect sizes
methodology.ablations: None (profile, RAG and critique node not ablated)
methodology.contamination_controls: Comments removed; snippets and oracle docstrings come from public CodeSearchNet, so the model has likely seen them

standards.peer_review: Accepted at ICSME 2026 Tool Demonstration and Data Showcase track (short paper)
standards.artifacts: Tool repository and demo video; study data, questionnaires and grading sheets not stated as released

biases.detail: 18 participants, 4 snippets; authors themselves attribute the p=0.085 to low power.
Isolated snippets with comments stripped, not comprehension of an unfamiliar codebase.
Embedding cosine against docstrings cannot separate conditions; workload and personalisation were measured only in the treatment arm, against a scale midpoint.
A no-AI control cannot test the paper's contributions (profile conditioning, in-editor anchoring) against a plain LLM explanation.
Authors graded correctness and supervised every session; grading not blinded to condition.
Abstract reports a non-significant speed-up and an uncompared workload reduction as findings.
CodeSearchNet snippets and docstrings are public.
Table II means at or above the midpoint are reported as significantly below it; t(16) degrees of freedom do not match 18 paired participants.

coi.affiliations: University of Salerno (SeSa Lab); Aalborg University
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None; TARS is the authors' research tool (uses OpenAI GPT-4.1 Nano)
coi.detail: No vendor interest; authors evaluate their own tool.

verdict_reason: The body supports none of the three abstract claims. The speed-up is not significant, workload was never compared with the control, and personalisation was never ablated. Unpaired tests on paired data and Table II numbers that contradict their own significance statements add to this. The only usable signal is a weak null: LLM explanations did not improve snippet comprehension correctness.
applicability: The question is exactly the onboarding one: does an in-IDE explainer help a developer without context understand Java code? But the answer here is 'no measurable comprehension gain on four snippets with a nano model', and nothing is learned about profile-tailored explanations. Do not cite this as evidence that personalised explain modes help onboarding. If the team builds a walkthrough or explain mode into the harness, measure comprehension with a follow-up task done without the tool (as 2607.26375 did), compare against a plain chat explanation to isolate any profile effect, and treat lower self-reported effort as a possible risk rather than a benefit.

conflicts_with.detail: Tension rather than direct contradiction: TARS presents lower self-reported mental effort as a benefit, while 2607.26375 finds that low-effort AI interaction correlates with lower comprehension of one's own code and that agent users score lower on comprehension. The interventions differ (explainer vs code-editing agent).
